accuracy.reason: Eight linked primary URLs were checked. EBS lifetime/deletion and intra-zone replication are scoped correctly; attachment does not imply formatting or filesystem coordination. fsync scope includes private-buffer and directory-entry limits. Snapshots exclude cached bytes and are asynchronous without a claim of automatic application consistency. No false guarantee found.

evidence.quote: A volume restored from a snapshot can already contain a filesystem and valuable data. Formatting it overwrites filesystem structures and can destroy access to that data. Successful attachment gives no reason to run a format operation automatically.

Persistent storage can retain delivered data after a process stops or an instance's running life ends. The service lifecycle and deletion policy still matter. Amazon EBS volumes can outlive an EC2 instance, but its delete-on-termination setting can remove a volume when the instance terminates. Inspect the actual setting instead of assuming it survives.

The operation's scope matters: syncing a file does not necessarily persist its directory entry; Linux may also require syncing the containing directory. Follow the supported procedure for the operation and storage stack instead of treating one call as a universal recipe.

A snapshot preserves a volume's state at a point in time. EBS snapshots capture data written to the volume, excluding bytes still in application or operating-system caches. During an application update, the stored state may contain only some related writes.

mechanisms.reason: All eight objectives have causal teaching: addressed ranges versus filesystem/database layers; allocation/attachment/format/mount and destructive formatting; persistence versus deletion/placement; volatile-to-durable write path; conflicting independent filesystem caches; partial on-volume state versus application recovery; operations/bytes/queue/host bottlenecks; interface choice and retained operator duties. Layer and shared-cache diagrams accurately illustrate these mechanisms, without universalizing the database-on-files path.

evidence.quote: A filesystem organizes blocks into files, directories and metadata. A database using those files adds records, queries and transaction rules. These are layers with different responsibilities: a database can use block storage without the volume becoming a database.

Writes can pass through volatile application buffers and operating-system caches before reaching persistent storage. An ordinary buffered write can report success while recent bytes remain only in memory. A host crash can lose those bytes; a persistent volume cannot preserve data that never reached it.

An ordinary single-host filesystem assumes it controls its disk structures. Two independent mounts can each cache an old view and make conflicting updates, overwriting metadata or data. Attachment can succeed while concurrent writing is unsafe. AWS explicitly warns that ordinary XFS and EXT4 filesystems are not designed for simultaneous access from multiple servers.

Measure a representative workload: its request sizes, demand, latency and queued requests. A queue holds operations waiting for completion; excessive demand can increase that wait. Compare both volume limits and the host's storage-path limits. EBS, for example, can be limited by the instance's bandwidth as well as the volume.

coherence.reason: The sequence teaches the device and higher layers before safe preparation, lifecycle before flush scope, caches before unsafe sharing and snapshots, then performance and interface choice. The layer diagram labels its path as one common path, and the sharing diagram accurately shows uncoordinated caches. Each card supplies prerequisites for later decisions; no recurring scenario is needed.

evidence.quote: Attaching a volume makes its device accessible to a host. It does not create a filesystem, mount it or start a database. The diagram shows a common database-on-files path; software designed for raw block access can use a different path.

Formatting creates a filesystem. Mounting makes that filesystem accessible at a location in the host's directory tree. For file use, format only the verified empty intended volume; mount a suitable existing filesystem without formatting it again.

A database may be able to repair or replay a disk state as it would after a crash. That is different from an application-consistent backup prepared at a valid application boundary. Snapshot success alone proves neither a complete transaction nor that the application can recover.

Choosing block storage leaves filesystem or database management, safe attachment, deletion settings, capacity, performance and tested recovery to the system's operators. Choose by access pattern, sharing and recovery needs, not just by the familiarity of a disk.

decisions.reason: The reader can choose inspect-versus-format, audit deletion and placement, use supported durability completion, reject unsafe multi-mounting, prepare and test historical recovery points, and diagnose host versus volume limits before spending. Interface choice includes what block storage leaves to operators. These are practical bounded decisions, not a product list.

evidence.quote: Formatting creates a filesystem. Mounting makes that filesystem accessible at a location in the host's directory tree. For file use, format only the verified empty intended volume; mount a suitable existing filesystem without formatting it again.

If the requirement is simply shared files and directories, consider a shared file service. Shared block access needs a filesystem or application expressly designed to coordinate it. Verify both provider attachment support and the software's coordination requirements; enabling a volume option does not supply those rules.

Restore into a volume, attach it appropriately and use its existing filesystem without formatting. Retain historical points that meet your recovery needs: a snapshot taken after a damaging update may preserve the damage. Test restoration and application usability, including how much data and recovery time you can afford to lose.
If the host or another part of the application is the bottleneck, buying more volume performance may not reduce application latency. Find where the time goes before changing the setting.

evidence.quote: Use the application's or database's supported durability procedure. It must send the relevant buffered data onward, wait for the required completion and handle errors. On Linux, fsync flushes a file's data and relevant metadata toward durable storage and waits for the device's completion report. It cannot flush bytes still held only in an application's own buffer.

A database may be able to repair or replay a disk state as it would after a crash. That is different from an application-consistent backup prepared at a valid application boundary. Snapshot success alone proves neither a complete transaction nor that the application can recover.

Capacity measures how much data fits. IOPS counts input/output operations per second. Throughput measures bytes transferred per second. I/O latency is the time one operation takes to complete. More capacity alone does not guarantee faster access.
